name: Alexander Hamilton
role: First U.S. Secretary of the Treasury (1789-1795) and Federalist leader
summary: Hamilton argued for a strong national government with an energetic executive, an independent judiciary and a Senate and executive serving long terms. As Treasury Secretary he funded the national debt, founded a national bank on implied powers, and urged protective duties and bounties for manufactures. He opposed slavery, helped found the New York Manumission Society and welcomed immigration, while distrusting democratic excess and favoring British-style stability.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Federalists 23 to 26 argue that the Union needs armies and fleets, with powers over them left without limitation.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: His record: he proposed the First Bank of the United States, chartered in 1791 as the government's fiscal agent issuing a national paper currency.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Federalist 84 calls the prohibition of titles of nobility the corner-stone of republican government and his 1786 Cincinnati report objected to hereditary membership as referring to birth what belongs to merit, but in June 1787 he praised the House of Lords as a most noble institution.

abolish-ip.rationale: The Report on Manufactures proposes rewards and premiums to induce useful inventions and improvements, so he favored legal incentives for inventors over abolishing patents.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The Examination No. VIII asks that aliens be given time to get rid of foreign and acquire American attachments and to imbibe the spirit of the government, and warns that they bring the customs and manners of their native country.

ban-interest.rationale: His record: as Treasury Secretary he borrowed at Amsterdam on interest-bearing loans and set up a national bank whose notes entered circulation through lending.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Federalist 26 defends the Constitution's rule that appropriations for military purposes lapse after two years, so the legislature must keep deciding on the funds.

central-bank-independence.rationale: His Report on a National Bank says the bank must be under a private, not a public, direction so that government necessity cannot abuse its credit, and warns that government paper emissions would inflate the currency.

conscription.rationale: In his 3 September 1780 letter to Duane he urged recruiting the army on the Swedish model, by drafting by lot within classes of inhabitants, and wanted the Confederation to provide for it by a fundamental law.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Federalist 22 says the American government must rest on the consent of the people, the pure original fountain of all legitimate authority.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: Federalist 83 holds trial by jury in high estimation and treats jury trial in criminal cases, provided for in the Constitution, as the essential guard, but denies an inseparable connection between liberty and civil jury trial.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Federalist 78 says courts must declare acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution void, since limits on legislative authority can be kept in no other way.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: His record: he built the federal revenue on customs duties and excises, and in 1794 sent the militia army to enforce the excise on distilled spirits.

decide-locally.rationale: At the Convention he proposed subordinating the states and asked what use the state apparatus served; by Federalist 17 he accepted states keeping local authority but wanted national matters handled nationally.

democracy-best.rationale: At the Convention he noted that even tenacious republicans decried the vices of democracy and proposed life tenure for the executive and senate, though in the Federalist he defended a republican government resting on the people.

democratic-peace.rationale: Federalist 6 says the ancient republics (Sparta, Athens, Rome, Carthage) were as often at war as neighboring monarchies, and that commerce adds new incentives for war.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Federalist 68 defends choosing the president through electors chosen by the people for the purpose, rather than by a direct popular vote or by an existing body.

direct-votes.rationale: At the 1788 New York ratifying convention he denied that pure democracy would be the most perfect government, saying the ancient democracies in which the people themselves deliberated never possessed one feature of good government.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The Examination No. VIII says an influx of foreigners produces a heterogeneous compound, that whatever tends to a discordant intermixture is injurious, and that incorporating many foreigners had already divided the community.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Farmer Refuted says that the origin of all justly established civil government must be a voluntary compact between rulers and ruled, asking what title any man can have to govern others except their own consent.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Federalist 11 and 12 argue for active foreign commerce and a navy; the Report on Manufactures seeks independence in military and essential supplies without shutting off trade.

elective-rulers.rationale: His Convention plan had an executive chosen by electors, not hereditary, and Federalist 69 stresses that the president would be elected, unlike a hereditary king.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Federalist 84 argues that a bill of rights is unnecessary and even dangerous in the proposed Constitution, while noting the Constitution already bars bills of attainder and ex post facto laws.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1779 letter calls their natural faculties as good as ours and cites the dictates of humanity for emancipation through service, but it proposes freedom only with the sword and no equal civil rights.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: His 1790 and 1795 reports on public credit ask that it be made a fundamental maxim that the creation of debt should always be accompanied with the means of extinguishment, binding the government against unfunded borrowing.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The Examination No. VIII proposes that the rights of acquiring property be conferred on aliens at once on declaring their intention to become citizens, postponing only political privileges.

free-trade.rationale: He treats freedom of trade as a general rule but argues for protecting duties, bounties and, in Federalist 11, exclusion of British shipping as retaliation, so the record points both ways.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Federalist 74 says the direction of war most peculiarly demands power exercised by a single hand, and Federalist 76 defends the President's power to nominate officers as better lodged in one man than in a body.

hereditarian-race.rationale: In his 14 March 1779 letter to John Jay he answered the objection that Black men were too stupid to be soldiers by saying their natural faculties are as good as ours, and blamed the contempt whites had been taught for them.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: His record: the bank he proposed was 80% owned by private investors and lent its notes into circulation, a profit-seeking bank rather than one owned by its borrowers.

land-value-tax.rationale: Advising Sedgwick on the 1798 direct tax, he wanted a land tax only as an auxiliary, preferred throwing the weight on houses because lands were harder to manage, and added stamp, succession and import duties.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Report on Manufactures answers the argument that industry left alone finds its best channel by urging active government encouragement of manufactures, calling for exceptions to a policy of leaving trade alone.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: In his 1799 letter to Dayton he called the Virginia and Kentucky effort to unite state legislatures in direct resistance to laws of the Union nothing less than an attempt to change the government, and urged vigorous counteraction.

minority-veto.rationale: Federalist 22 says giving a minority a negative upon the majority is a poison that subjects the sense of the greater number to the lesser, citing the Polish diet where a single vote could stop everything.

mixed-constitution.rationale: On June 18, 1787 he praised the British constitution for uniting public strength with individual security and proposed an elected assembly alongside a life-tenure Senate and executive.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: On June 18, 1787 he said in private that the British government, with its hereditary monarch, was the best in the world, while in Federalist 69 he stressed that the president, unlike a king, would be elected.

more-religion-public.rationale: In April 1802 he proposed to Bayard a Christian Constitutional Society whose first object was the support of the Christian religion, joined to electioneering and charities; he proposed no legal role for religion.

nation-first.rationale: Pacificus No. IV (1793) holds that a nation's duty to make its own welfare the guide of its actions is stronger than an individual's, and that a policy regulated by its own interest, as far as justice and good faith permit, ought to prevail.

natural-rulers.rationale: In Yates's report of his 18 June 1787 speech he said communities divide into the rich and well-born and the mass of the people, that the people seldom judge or determine right, and that the first class should have a distinct, permanent share in government.

night-watchman-state.rationale: His record: besides defense and justice, his Treasury chartered a national bank as fiscal agent and currency issuer and built a revenue system of customs and excises to fund the full repayment of the war debt.

no-central-bank.rationale: His record: he proposed the First Bank of the United States, which opened in 1791 as the government's fiscal agent and issued a national paper currency.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Tully No. III (1794) calls an inviolable respect for the Constitution and laws the most sacred duty in a republic and says those who undermine the authority of the laws lead from freedom to slavery.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: His January 1795 report calls it a sacred obligation to extinguish the actual debt with reasonable celerity, though his 1790 report held that a properly funded debt would be a national blessing.

people-in-arms.rationale: Federalist 25 says reliance on the militia as the natural bulwark nearly cost independence, and Federalists 24 to 26 defend a regular national army.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Examination No. IX (1802) attacks admitting immigrants straight to citizenship as breaking down every pale erected for the preservation of a national spirit and a national character.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: In the first Letter from Phocion (1784) he wrote that the legislature cannot, without tyranny, punish or disfranchise citizens without trial and conviction of offences known by laws previously established, calling this a fundamental principle of law and liberty.

property-franchise.rationale: His 1787 draft constitution gives every free male citizen of 21 an equal vote for the Assembly but limits the electors of the Senate to holders of an estate in land, so it both rejects and applies a property qualification.

property-fundamental.rationale: His Vindication of the Funding System calls the rights of private property sacred and admits exceptions to the general rules of property only for necessity; his 1790 report rejected discrimination against bondholders as a breach of contract.

public-money-creation.rationale: His record: the bank he proposed was 80% privately owned and put its paper currency into circulation through lending, while a public mint coined specie.

recall-officials.rationale: At the New York ratifying convention he opposed the amendment letting state legislatures recall senators, saying that whoever held the power of recall, the senator would live in a state of vassalage and lose the firmness his duty required.

recallable-delegates.rationale: In June 1788 he argued that a senator is not simply the agent of his State but an agent for the Union, bound to serve the good of the whole though his State should condemn him, and opposed both recall and compulsory rotation.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The 1791 Report on Manufactures urged opening every possible avenue to emigration, but in 1802 (The Examination No. VIII) he warned that an influx of foreigners breeds a heterogeneous compound and that native population growth was now enough; that essay argued only over naturalization terms.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: His 1787 plan had state governors appointed by the general government with a veto on state laws, but Federalist 17 denies that the Union would absorb the residuary authorities left to the states for local purposes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Federalist 28 says that if representatives betray their constituents there is no resource but the original right of self-defense, paramount to all positive forms of government, against the usurpations of national rulers.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Pacificus No. IV says a government can rarely if ever be justified in indulging generosity at the expense of its nation's interest, and limits national benevolence to good offices that cost the nation no real detriment.

right-to-secede.rationale: In his last letter (to Sedgwick, 10 July 1804) he wrote that dismemberment of the Union would be a clear sacrifice of great advantages without any counterbalancing good.

second-chamber.rationale: His Convention plan had a Senate holding office during good behavior; Federalist 65 and 66 defend the Senate as part of the proposed Constitution.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: His record: as Treasury Secretary he raised the young republic's funds through loans negotiated with bankers at Amsterdam.

separated-powers.rationale: Federalists 65, 70, 73 and 78 defend distinct departments with checks, including the presidential veto, an independent judiciary and impeachment.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Federalist 70 names a due responsibility among the ingredients of safety, and Federalists 65 and 69 make the president liable to impeachment and removal.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: His record: his Treasury made repaying the war debt in full its first priority and drew on new Amsterdam loans to meet the foreign debt, rather than seeking its cancellation.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Report on Manufactures proposes public bounties, premiums and a fund to induce and direct capital and skilled labor into manufactures judged important to national independence.

state-harmful.rationale: Federalist 15 says government was instituted because men's passions will not conform to reason and justice without constraint.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: As Pacificus he defended the 1793 neutrality proclamation, saying the nation's true interest lies in preserving peace and staying out of the European war.

strong-leader.rationale: Federalist 70 calls energy in the executive a leading character of good government and he urged a strong executive on June 18, 1787, but always within law and impeachment, not as bypassing the legislature.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Phocion (1784) condemned disfranchising or banishing whole classes of political opponents without trial, but in 1799 he urged federal prosecution of seditious libels against officers and asked why alien editors of incendiary presses were not sent away.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Report on Manufactures recommends protecting duties on foreign articles that rival domestic ones, though it advises using prohibitions and very high duties only sparingly and prefers bounties.

taxation-theft.rationale: Federalist 30 calls money the vital principle of the body politic and says a general power of taxation must be built into the government.

term-limits.rationale: Federalist 72 argues at length against excluding the chief magistrate from re-election, temporarily or permanently.

territorial-expansion.rationale: On 26 January 1799 he wrote to Otis that he had long considered acquiring the Floridas and Louisiana essential to the permanency of the Union and urged taking possession of them, and he backed detaching South America from Spain.

universal-morality.rationale: The Farmer Refuted (1775) holds that God constituted an eternal and immutable law of nature, discernible by reason and binding over all the globe, in all countries and at all times.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: In The Farmer Refuted he adopts Blackstone's view that no human laws are of any validity if contrary to the law of nature, and says dominion usurped against the people's consent confers no obligation to obedience.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Federalist 72 defends re-eligibility and argues that excluding a chief magistrate from office would be pernicious; Federalist 69 has the president re-eligible as often as the people choose.

women-suffrage.rationale: His 1787 draft constitution confines the vote for the Assembly to the free male citizens and inhabitants of the states.

notes: Born 1755 or 1757. Second pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-07): read his own texts in full in the Lodge Federal Edition (archive.org scans, vols. 1-10, kept in scratchpad/sources/alexander-hamilton/) and the Gutenberg J. C. Hamilton vol. 1, plus Treasury and Federal Reserve History pages for the Treasury record. Founders Online refused scripted access (AWS WAF bot challenge), so it was not used. Searched every theme: economy (bank, public credit, loans, manufactures, taxes), government (NY ratifying convention, 1787 draft constitution, Federalist, Virginia and Kentucky resolutions, secession), world (Pacificus, Quasi-War letters), society and culture (Examination of 1802 on immigrants, 1779 letter on Black soldiers), liberty (Phocion, Tully, Farmer Refuted). Answers that rested on Wikipedia were re-sourced to his own texts or nulled; where his Treasury or military record bears on a statement it answers alone. His view of immigration hardened by 1802 (Examination VIII), which made reduce-immigration mixed. The Farewell Address draft was not used: he wrote it in Washington's voice. Ecology and technology statements are anachronistic for him.
